claim: Lymph nodes (LNs) are a common site of metastasis in solid cancers.
source: Lymph nodes (LNs) are a common site of metastasis in solid cancers
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, supported by citation to Nathanson, 2003

claim: Cutaneous melanomas show inherent properties of LN colonization.
source: cutaneous melanomas show inherent properties of LN colonization
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract

claim: Siglec1-expressing subcapsular sinus (SCS) macrophages provide anchorage to pioneer metastatic cells.
source: We show that Siglec1-expressing subcapsular sinus (SCS) macrophages provide anchorage to pioneer metastatic cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by microscopy data showing physical contact between cancer cells and SCS macrophages (Figure 1A, B, Video 1)

claim: Interactions between hypersialylated cancer cells and Siglec1 drive the proliferation of cancer cells.
source: We performed in vitro co-culture to demonstrate that interactions between hypersialylated cancer cells and Siglec1 drive the proliferation of cancer cells.
evidence: This is supported by co-culture experiments showing increased Ki67 expression in cancer cells cultured with Siglec1-expressing cells (Figure 2F, G)

claim: Siglec1-interacting cancer cells show enrichment in positive regulators of cell cycle progression compared to non-Siglec1-interacting cancer cells.
source: When comparing the transcriptome profile of Siglec1-interacting cancer cells against non-Siglec1-interacting cancer cells, we detected enrichment in positive regulators of cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data and pathway analysis (Figure 3C, D, E)

claim: Knockout of St3gal3 sialyltransferase compromised the metastatic efficiency of tumor cells by reducing α−2,3-linked sialylation.
source: Further, knockout of St3gal3 sialyltransferase compromised the metastatic efficiency of tumor cells by reducing α−2,3-linked sialylation.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo metastasis experiments showing reduced LN metastasis burden in St3gal3 KO cells (Figure 5C-E)

claim: The interaction between Siglec1-expressing SCS macrophages and pioneer metastatic cells drives cell cycle progression and enables efficient metastatic colonization.
source: Thus, the interaction between Siglec1-expressing SCS macrophages and pioneer metastatic cells drives cell cycle progression and enables efficient metastatic colonization.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings including proliferation assays, transcriptome analysis, and in vivo metastasis studies

claim: LN metastasis is often associated with the severity of the disease.
source: Lymphatic dissemination is a common metastasis route in solid cancers and LN metastasis is often associated with the severity of the disease (Nathanson, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation

claim: Melanoma metastasizes to LNs very early in cancer progression.
source: Melanoma metastasizes to LNs very early in cancer progression
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations (Werner-Klein et al., 2018)

claim: Metastatic cells acquire driver genetic changes during colonization of LNs.
source: metastatic cells acquire driver genetic changes during colonization of LNs, suggesting the important role that LNs have in tumor evolution (Werner-Klein et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated based on citation to Werner-Klein et al., 2018

claim: Post-LN-colonizing cancer cells with acquired colonization signatures show superior xenograft formation in mice compared with pre-colonizing cancer cells.
source: These evolved post-LN-colonizing cancer cells with acquired colonization signatures show superior xenograft formation in mice compared with pre-colonizing cancer cells
evidence: This is stated based on citation to Werner-Klein et al., 2018

claim: During LN colonization metastatic cells gain access to the blood vessels in LNs and take a hematogenous route to colonize peripheral organs.
source: Besides lymphatic dissemination to downstream LNs, during LN colonization metastatic cells gain access to the blood vessels in LNs and take a hematogenous route to colonize peripheral organs (Pereira et al., 2018; Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to Pereira et al., 2018 and Brown et al., 2018

claim: Distal organ metastatic colonization process is organ-specific and requires interactions between disseminated tumor cells (DTCs; seed) and distal organs (soil) to reinitiate growth.
source: The distal organ metastatic colonization process is organ-specific and requires interactions between disseminated tumor cells (DTCs; seed) and distal organs (soil) to reinitiate growth (Peinado et al., 2017; Massagué and Obenauf, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations

claim: Very few early DTCs eventually form distal metastasis despite primary tumors releasing many early DTCs into the circulation.
source: Although primary tumors release many early DTCs into the circulation, which are the precursors of metastasis, very few eventually form distal metastasis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: The majority of DTCs that land in unfamiliar distal sites fail to survive the hostile microenvironment of the new-found stroma.
source: The majority of DTCs that land in unfamiliar distal sites fail to survive the hostile microenvironment of the new-found stroma.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Distal organ colonization is a bottleneck of the metastasis colonization process.
source: This inefficiency of metastasis suggests that distal organ colonization is a bottleneck of the metastasis colonization process.
evidence: This is inferred from the inefficiency of metastasis described in the previous sentences

claim: Pioneer metastatic cells require active participation of the host stroma to obtain survival and viability signals to gain a foothold in new landing sites.
source: To gain a foothold in new landing sites, pioneer metastatic cells require active participation of the host stroma to obtain survival and viability signals (Mehlen and Puisieux, 2006; Buchheit et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations

claim: LN metastatic colonization begins with the arrest of metastatic cells in the LN subcapsular sinus (SCS).
source: The current paradigm posits that LN metastatic colonization begins with the arrest of metastatic cells in the LN subcapsular sinus (SCS) (Das et al., 2013; Jeong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations

claim: Pioneer metastatic cells could be observed in the SCS of sentinel popliteal LNs lined by Lyve-1+ lymphatic endothelial cells as early as 2 weeks after inoculation and before the appearance of any visible macroscopic metastatic foci.
source: Pioneer metastatic cells could be observed in the SCS of sentinel popliteal LNs lined by Lyve-1+ lymphatic endothelial cells as early as 2 weeks after inoculation and before the appearance of any visible macroscopic metastatic foci (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Siglec1 is primarily expressed on SCS and medullary sinus macrophages in LNs.
source: by depleting LN-resident macrophages through injecting clodronate liposomes into the mouse footpads, we confirmed that Siglec1 is primarily expressed on SCS and medullary sinus macrophages in LNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using clodronate liposome depletion shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Pioneer metastatic cells are found in close contact with SCS macrophages within the LN SCS.
source: We found the pioneer metastatic cells in close contact with SCS macrophages within the LN SCS, suggesting they interact with each other right after metastastic cells enter the SCS (Figure 1A and B; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A, B and Video 1

claim: After initial cancer cell attachment to SCS macrophages, small metastatic foci developed within the SCS.
source: We analyzed the sections from day 17 to day 21, and found that after initial cancer cell attachment to SCS macrophages, small metastatic foci developed within the SCS (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C

claim: With the increase in size, the metastatic foci exerted pressure on the SCS macrophage–lymphatic lining, which eventually lead to disruption of the sinus lining and metastatic cells entering the LN cortex.
source: With the increase in size, the foci exerted pressure on the SCS macrophage–lymphatic lining, which eventually lead to disruption of the sinus lining and metastatic cells entering the LN cortex (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Breast cancer cells (4T1) also used SCS macrophages to find a foothold in LNs.
source: to test the generalizability of our observations, we implanted an EGFP-expressing 4T1 mouse breast cancer cell line into mouse footpads and found that breast cancer cells also used SCS macrophages to find a foothold in LNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Other tumors metastasizing to LNs may also use a LN colonization mechanism similar to melanoma.
source: our observations indicate that other tumors metastasizing to LNs may also use a LN colonization mechanism similar to melanoma
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that breast cancer cells also interact with SCS macrophages and from previous observations cited (Das et al., 2013; Jeong et al., 2015)

claim: Increased protein sialylation is characteristic of several cancer types including melanomas.
source: Increased protein sialylation is characteristic of several cancer types including melanomas (Kim and Varki, 1997; Agrawal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations

claim: B16F10 melanoma cells show more than 10-fold higher cell surface α2,3‐ and α2,6‐linked sialylation compared with non-tumorigenic mouse melanocytes (melan-A cell line).
source: we found more than 10-fold higher cell surface α2,3‐ and α2,6‐linked sialylation in B16F10 melanoma cells compared with non-tumorigenic mouse melanocytes, melan-A cell line (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D)
evidence: This is supported by lectin staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D

claim: Melan-A cells showed only basal levels of α2,3-sialylation.
source: Of note, melan-A cells showed only basal levels of α2,3-sialylation.
evidence: This is stated based on the lectin staining data

claim: Siglec1 is a sialic-acid-recognizing protein that interacts with α2,3‐ and α2,6‐linked sialylated proteins.
source: As Siglec1 is a sialic-acid-recognizing protein that interacts with α2,3‐ and α2,6‐linked sialylated proteins (Crocker et al., 1999)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation

claim: B16-GFP cells show significantly higher adherence to Siglec1-expressing HEK293T cells compared with mock-transfected cells.
source: We found significantly higher adherence of B16-GFP cells to Siglec1-expressing HEK293T cells compared with mock-transfected cells (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by cell adhesion assay data shown in Figure 1E, F

claim: Treatment with sialidase abolished the Siglec1 binding to cancer cells while removing the α2,3‐ sialylation completely and α2,6- sialylation by one third.
source: Furthermore, treatment with sialidase abolished the Siglec1 binding to cancer cells while removing the α2,3‐ sialylation completely and α2,6- sialylation by one third, suggesting Siglec1 preferentially binds to α2,3‐sialylated protein on cancer cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–F).
evidence: This is supported by sialidase treatment experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–F

claim: Siglec1 preferentially binds to α2,3‐sialylated protein on cancer cells.
source: suggesting Siglec1 preferentially binds to α2,3‐sialylated protein on cancer cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–F)
evidence: This is inferred from the sialidase treatment data showing complete removal of α2,3-sialylation abolished Siglec1 binding

claim: Siglec1-expressing SCS macrophages provide the 'soil' for incoming metastatic cells and prevent their washout with lymph flow.
source: Based on the above in vivo and in vitro results, we suggest that Siglec1-expressing SCS macrophages provide the 'soil' for incoming metastatic cells and prevent their washout with lymph flow.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the in vivo and in vitro experimental data showing physical interaction and adhesion

claim: Disseminated tumor cells (DTCs) land in distal metastasis sites with limited chances of survival.
source: With limited chances of survival, disseminated tumor cells (DTCs) land in distal metastasis sites (Massagué and Obenauf, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation

claim: Pioneer metastatic cells must overcome anoikis and amorphosis, and resume proliferation by establishing adhesive and signaling interactions with host tissue to establish a new colony.
source: To establish a new colony, pioneer metastatic cells must overcome anoikis and amorphosis, and resume proliferation by establishing adhesive and signaling interactions with host tissue (Mehlen and Puisieux, 2006; Buchheit et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations

claim: Pioneer metastatic cells were in a non-proliferative non-apoptotic state when they landed in the LN SCS.
source: We used apoptosis marker cleaved-caspase-3 and cell proliferation marker Ki67 to determine the proliferation status of pioneer metastatic cells and found that they were in a non-proliferative non-apoptotic state when they landed in the LN SCS
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical staining data for cleaved-caspase-3 and Ki67

claim: Pioneer metastatic cells resumed proliferation after they came into contact with SCS macrophages.
source: and resumed proliferation after they came into contact with SCS macrophages (Figure 2A–D)
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 2A–D

claim: Siglec1 expression did not affect the proliferation status of HEK293T cells.
source: Of note, Siglec1 expression did not affect the proliferation status of HEK293T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Cancer cells cultured in non-adherent conditions showed significantly reduced Ki67 expression, similar to DTCs.
source: Of note, we observed that cancer cells cultured in non-adherent conditions showed significantly reduced Ki67 expression, similar to DTCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D) (Pantel and Brakenhoff, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D

claim: More Ki67+ proliferating B16-GFP cells were found in tumor cells-HEKSiglec1 co-cultures compared with cells co-cultured with HEKMock.
source: We found more Ki67+ proliferating B16-GFP cells in tumor cells-HEKSiglec1 co-cultures compared with cells co-cultured with HEKMock (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is supported by co-culture experiment data shown in Figure 2F, G

claim: Conditioned media from HEKMock and HEKSiglec1 cells did not affect the proliferation of B16-GFP cells.
source: To exclude the possibility that expression of Siglec1 may induce HEK293T cells to secrete some pro-proliferation factors and in turn induce B16-GFP cell proliferation, we prepared conditioned media from HEKMock and HEKSiglec1 cells and treated the B16-GFP cells in a similar setting as the co-culture experiments. Conditioned media did not affect the proliferation of B16-GFP cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, F

claim: B16-GFP cells co-cultured with HEKSiglec1 cells had significantly lower Annexin V-positive apoptotic cells.
source: B16-GFP cells co-cultured with HEKSiglec1 cells had significantly lower Annexin V-positive apoptotic cells (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 2H, I

claim: B16-GFP cells co-cultured with Siglec1 knockdown J774A.1 macrophages showed decreased proliferation compared with B16-GFP cells co-cultured with control siRNA-transfected macrophages.
source: We observed decreased proliferation of B16-GFP cells co-cultured with these Siglec1 knockdown J774A.1 macrophages compared with B16-GFP cells co-cultured with control siRNA-transfected macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by co-culture experiment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F

claim: There was a significant increase in Annexin V-positive apoptotic cancer cells when they were co-cultured with Siglec1-knocked down macrophages.
source: Furthermore, we observed a significant increase in Annexin V-positive apoptotic cancer cells when they were co-cultured with Siglec1-knocked down macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G,H).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G, H

claim: Siglec1 has a role in cancer cell survival and proliferation during the initial metastatic colonization of LNs by pioneer metastatic cells.
source: Taken together, our data revealed a role for Siglec1 in cancer cell survival and proliferation during the initial metastatic colonization of LNs by pioneer metastatic cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from multiple experimental results showing increased proliferation and decreased apoptosis in Siglec1-interacting cancer cells

claim: Successful metastatic colonization requires activation of the pro-survival PI3K/AKT and ERK pathways.
source: Successful metastatic colonization requires activation of the pro-survival PI3K/AKT and ERK pathways (Buchheit et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation

claim: Siglec1 engagement with cancer cells induced AKT phosphorylation at S473, which is a PI3K-mediated AKT-activating event.
source: Siglec1 engagement with cancer cells induced AKT phosphorylation at S473, which is a PI3K-mediated AKT-activating event (Figure 2J,K).
evidence: This is supported by Phosflow analysis data shown in Figure 2J, K

claim: Higher levels of phosphorylated ERK1/2 (ERK1, T203/Y205; ERK2, T183/Y185) were found in cancer cells co-cultured with HEKSiglec1.
source: Furthermore, in a similar setting, we found higher levels of phosphorylated ERK1/2 (ERK1, T203/Y205; ERK2, T183/Y185; Figure 2L,M) in cancer cells co-cultured with HEKSiglec1.
evidence: This is supported by Phosflow analysis data shown in Figure 2L, M

claim: B16-GFP cells co-cultured with Siglec1-knocked down J774A.1 cells showed reduced AKT and ERK1/2 phosphorylation in comparison with cells co-cultured with J774A.1 cells transfected with control siRNA.
source: Consistent with the reduced proliferation and increased apoptosis in B16-GFP co-cultured with Siglec1-knocked down J774A.1 cells, we found reduced AKT and ERK1/2 phosphorylation in comparison with cells co-cultured with J774A.1 cells transfected with control siRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I–L).
evidence: This is supported by Phosflow analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2I–L

claim: Siglec1 interactions provide growth cues to cancer cells.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that Siglec1 interactions provide growth cues to cancer cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing increased AKT and ERK1/2 phosphorylation in Siglec1-interacting cancer cells

claim: Siglec1 interactions may facilitate the LN colonization of melanoma cells.
source: Therefore, these interactions may facilitate the LN colonization of melanoma cells.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed growth cues provided by Siglec1 interactions

claim: Tumor cells cultured with HEKSiglec1 showed differential expression (fold change >1.5; raw P<0.05) of 239 genes, of which 68 were upregulated and 171 were downregulated compared with tumor cells that were not interacting with Siglec1.
source: Compared with tumor cells that were not interacting with Siglec1, tumor cells cultured with HEKSiglec1 showed differential expression (fold change >1.5; raw P<0.05) of 239 genes, of which 68 were upregulated and 171 were downregulated (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3B and source data 1

claim: Tumor cells from HEKSiglec1–tumor cell co-culture displayed enrichment in positive regulators of cell cycle and DNA replication compared with cancer cells cultured with mock-transfected HEK293T cells.
source: A pathway analysis of the upregulated genes revealed that tumor cells from HEKSiglec1–tumor cell co-culture displayed enrichment in positive regulators of cell cycle and DNA replication compared with cancer cells cultured with mock-transfected HEK293T cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Upregulated genes in Siglec1-interacting cancer cells were mainly involved in cell cycle-related biological processes.
source: Furthermore, gene ontology analysis revealed that upregulated genes were mainly involved in cell cycle-related biological processes (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3D, E

claim: RNA sequencing results confirmed higher levels of Ki67 expression in HEKSiglec1 co-cultured cancer cells.
source: Consistent with FACS analysis of Ki67 staining, RNA sequencing results confirmed higher levels of Ki67 expression in HEKSiglec1 co-cultured cancer cells (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3E and source data 1

claim: Downregulation of apoptosis-related (Bbc3, Rras, Ddit3, Ddit4) and tumor suppressor (Hes1, Ahnak, Timp3, Smad7, Ndrg1) genes was observed in Siglec1-interacting cancer cells.
source: Additionally, we observed downregulation of apoptosis-related (Bbc3, Rras, Ddit3, Ddit4) and tumor suppressor (Hes1, Ahnak, Timp3, Smad7, Ndrg1) genes in Siglec1-interacting cancer cells (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data in Figure 3—source data 1

claim: The interaction between Siglec1 and cancer cells drove cell cycle progression and proliferation in cancer cells.
source: Thus, the interaction between Siglec1 and cancer cells drove cell cycle progression and proliferation in cancer cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the transcriptome analysis showing enrichment in cell cycle genes

claim: Siglec1-mediated interactions between SCS macrophages and metastatic cells may provide the vital support required to overcome dormancy and initiate successful LN colonization.
source: In light of the prior knowledge of the vulnerabilities of metastatic processes, Siglec1-mediated interactions between SCS macrophages and metastatic cells may provide the vital support required to overcome dormancy and initiate successful LN colonization (Pantel and Brakenhoff, 2004; Sosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations to prior knowledge

claim: Gene expression data showed significant upregulation in cell cycle master regulator PLK1 expression in co-culture experiments.
source: Gene expression data showed significant upregulation in cell cycle master regulator PLK1 expression in co-culture experiments (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 1) (Paschal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3E and source data 1

claim: PLK1 phosphorylation at T210 is a mitosis-specific G2/M transition-activating event.
source: PLK1 phosphorylation at T210 is a mitosis-specific G2/M transition-activating event (Paschal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation

claim: LN metastatic cells showed 1.8-fold higher activation of PLK1 in comparison with primary tumor cells.
source: We found 1.8-fold higher activation of PLK1 in LN metastatic cells in comparison with primary tumor cells (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Phosflow analysis data shown in Figure 4A, B

claim: There was a marked increase in mitosis-committed cancer cells when B16-GFP cells were co-cultured with HEKSiglec1 in comparison with HEKMock.
source: Consistently, in in vitro experiments, we found marked increase in mitosis-committed cancer cells when B16-GFP cells were co-cultured with HEKSiglec1 in comparison with HEKMock (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by PLK1 phosphorylation data shown in Figure 4C, D

claim: Knockdown of Siglec1 significantly decreased PLK1 phosphorylation in B16-GFP cells co-cultured with J774A.1 macrophages.
source: With a reverse approach, where we knocked down Siglec1 using siRNA in J774A.1 macrophages and performed co-culture experiments with B16-GFP cells, we found that knockdown of Siglec1 significantly decreased PLK1 phosphorylation (Figure 4E–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E–G

claim: Siglec1-interacting tumor cells showed higher PLK1 phosphorylation than those that did not interact with Siglec1.
source: Taken together, Siglec1-interacting tumor cells showed higher PLK1 phosphorylation than those that did not interact with Siglec1.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the PLK1 phosphorylation experiments

claim: Strong mitotic induction observed in Siglec1-interacting tumor cells and confirmed by high PLK1 phosphorylation during early LN metastatic colonization supports the model whereby Siglec1 confers a growth advantage to pioneer metastatic cells.
source: This strong mitotic induction observed in Siglec1-interacting tumor cells and confirmed by high PLK1 phosphorylation during early LN metastatic colonization supports our model whereby Siglec1 confers a growth advantage to pioneer metastatic cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the PLK1 phosphorylation data

claim: The presence of a highly growth permissive 'soil' reflects the high prevalence of LN metastasis in melanoma during the early stages of primary tumor growth, even before metastasis to peripheral organs.
source: This presence of a highly growth permissive 'soil' reflects the high prevalence of LN metastasis in melanoma during the early stages of primary tumor growth, even before metastasis to peripheral organs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing growth-promoting interactions in LNs

claim: Hypersialylation in cancers, including melanomas, is directly linked to the metastatic potential of cancer cells.
source: Hypersialylation in cancers, including melanomas, is directly linked to the metastatic potential of cancer cells (Agrawal et al., 2017; Bos et al., 2009; Schultz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations

claim: ST3 beta-galactoside alpha-2,3-sialyltransferase 3 (St3gal3) is known to produce Siglec-binding α−2,3 sialylation in mice and is linked to metastasis and poor prognosis in several cancer types.
source: One sialyltransferase, ST3 beta-galactoside alpha-2,3-sialyltransferase 3 (St3gal3) is known to produce Siglec-binding α−2,3 sialylation in mice and is linked to metastasis and poor prognosis in several cancer types (Guo et al., 2011; Pérez-Garay et al., 2010; Cui et al., 2011; Chang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations

claim: St3gal3 knockout decreased α−2,3 sialylation of cell surface proteins by 20%.
source: Hence, we knocked out St3gal3 in B16-GFP cells using CRISPR-mediated single base pair deletion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), which decreased α−2,3 sialylation of cell surface proteins by 20% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by lectin staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D

claim: St3gal3 knockout cells showed approximately 70% reduced cell surface binding of Siglec1.
source: Additionally, St3gal3 knockout (KO) cells showed approximately 70% reduced cell surface binding of Siglec1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by Siglec1 binding data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F

claim: St3gal3 KO did not affect the proliferation of B16-GFP cells in culture, in vitro adhesion and migration, or growth as primary tumors.
source: Of note, St3gal3 KO did not affect the proliferation of B16-GFP cells in culture, in vitro adhesion and migration, or growth as primary tumors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–K)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–K

claim: St3gal3 KO abrogated the ability of B16-GFP to adhere to a Siglec1-expressing HEK293T cell monolayer.
source: but it abrogated the ability of B16-GFP to adhere to a Siglec1-expressing HEK293T cell monolayer (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by cell adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5A, B

claim: St3gal3 KO severely reduced the LN metastasis burden.
source: Notably, St3gal3 KO severely reduced the LN metastasis burden (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo metastasis data shown in Figure 5C–E

claim: No Siglec1 expression was found on primary tumor lymphatic vessels.
source: To explore the possibility of Siglec1 expression on primary tumor lymphatic vessels, which might have affected the initial egress of cancer cells from the primary tumor, we searched for Siglec1 expression on primary tumor lymphatic vessels and found none (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: St3gal3 KO B16-GFP cells are present in the LN SCS but did not form foci and were not in contact with SCS macrophages.
source: Immunohistological analysis at an early metastasis stage (day 17) revealed that although St3gal3 KO B16-GFP cells are present in the LN SCS, they did not form foci and were not in contact with SCS macrophages (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 5F

claim: WT B16-GFP cells formed tight-knit foci in contact with SCS macrophages.
source: Whereas, WT B16-GFP cells formed tight-knit foci in contact with SCS macrophages (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 5F

claim: St3gal3 KO B16-GFP cells showed severely reduced proliferation in the SCS in comparison with WT B16-GFP cells.
source: Ki67 staining revealed that St3gal3 KO B16-GFP cells showed severely reduced proliferation in the SCS in comparison with WT B16-GFP cells (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 staining data shown in Figure 5G, H

claim: Early metastatic cells originating from St3gal3 KO cells showed significantly decreased survival in the SCS.
source: Furthermore, early metastatic cells originating from St3gal3 KO cells showed significantly decreased survival in the SCS (Figure 5I,J).
evidence: This is supported by apoptosis marker staining data shown in Figure 5I, J

claim: St3gal3 KO tumors only formed small cell clusters, which crossed the SCS without growing in size in the SCS, suggesting a lack of ability to adhere to the SCS macrophages and hence reduced metastatic growth.
source: Three weeks after tumor cell implantation, a large metastatic focus had formed in the LN, which disrupted the SCS macrophages lining the LN sinus, but St3gal3 KO tumors only formed small cell clusters, which crossed the SCS without growing in size in the SCS, suggesting a lack of ability to adhere to the SCS macrophages and hence reduced metastatic growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and inferred from the observation

claim: Overall α−2,3-sialylation abundance on tumor cells affects the efficiency of LN metastasis formation.
source: Thus, overall α−2,3-sialylation abundance on tumor cells affects the efficiency of LN metastasis formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the St3gal3 knockout experiments showing reduced metastasis

claim: The survival and proliferation of pioneer metastatic cells in the LN SCS is a crucial process of metastatic colonization.
source: Combined, these results suggest that the survival and proliferation of pioneer metastatic cells in the LN SCS is crucial process of metastatic colonization
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing reduced metastasis when survival and proliferation are compromised

claim: Abrogation of SCS macrophage–tumor cell binding slowed down the metastatic colonization considerably.
source: and abrogation of SCS macrophage–tumor cell binding slowed down the metastatic colonization considerably
evidence: This is inferred from the St3gal3 knockout experiments showing reduced metastasis

claim: Melanoma has a predilection for metastasizing to LNs in the early stages of the disease.
source: Melanoma has a predilection for metastasizing to LNs in the early stages of the disease (Bedrosian et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citation

claim: The high prevalence of LN metastasis early during tumor progression suggests the presence of a metastasis-permissive environment in LNs.
source: The high prevalence of LN metastasis early during tumor progression suggests the presence of a metastasis-permissive environment in LNs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of high prevalence of early LN metastasis

claim: Lymphatic disseminated metastatic cells directly interact with SCS macrophages just after landing in the LN SCS.
source: We propose a model whereby lymphatic disseminated metastatic cells directly interact with SCS macrophages just after landing in the LN SCS.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental observations

claim: The overall abundance and continuous presence of Siglec1+ macrophages in the SCS facilitates efficient metastatic seeding by providing adherence and promoting cell cycle progression in otherwise vulnerable DTCs.
source: The overall abundance and continuous presence of Siglec1+ macrophages in the SCS facilitates efficient metastatic seeding by providing adherence and promoting cell cycle progression in otherwise vulnerable DTCs.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental observations

claim: The proposed model is in agreement with the sequence of events leading to metastatic colonization of LN observed by Das et al. and Jeong et al. using in vivo imaging.
source: Our model is in agreement with the sequence of events leading to metastatic colonization of LN observed by Das et al. and Jeong et al. using in vivo imaging, whereby they observed that pioneer metastatic cells remain in the LN SCS to form metastatic foci that grow in size and disrupts the SCS to invade the LN cortex (Das et al., 2013; Jeong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on agreement with cited literature

claim: LN SCS macrophages have been implicated in anti-tumor responses.
source: LN SCS macrophages have been implicated in anti-tumor responses (Asano et al., 2011; Pucci et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations

claim: Siglec1+ SCS macrophages physically interact with hypersialylated metastatic cells, conferring growth advantages upon them.
source: We show here another facet of Siglec1+ SCS macrophages where they physically interact with hypersialylated metastatic cells, conferring growth advantages upon them.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data showing physical interaction and increased proliferation

claim: Genes affected by Siglec1-cancer cell interactions were not only involved in cell cycle progression and DNA replication, but also in apoptosis and tumor suppression.
source: Genes affected by Siglec1-cancer cell interactions were not only involved in cell cycle progression and DNA replication, but also in apoptosis and tumor suppression.
evidence: This is supported by the transcriptome analysis data

claim: Reduced sialylation in tumor cells reduced the efficiency of metastasis.
source: Accordingly, reduced sialylation in tumor cells reduced the efficiency of metastasis.
evidence: This is supported by the St3gal3 knockout experiments

claim: The findings suggest how the organ-specific LN metastasis trait of melanoma arises.
source: Our findings also suggest how the organ-specific LN metastasis trait of melanoma arises
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing LN-specific interactions

claim: Countering hypersialylation may prove to be therapeutically beneficial in preventing LN metastasis and subsequent spread to distal organs.
source: and countering hypersialylation may therefore prove to be therapeutically beneficial in preventing LN metastasis and subsequent spread to distal organs.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings that reduced sialylation reduces metastasis
